g.passage: Consuelo opened the clock shop in Vigo every morning at seven, winding the wall clocks in the same order her late husband had used. Her nephew Aroha arrived from the coast in the spring of 1911 owing her forty pesetas, a sum he had borrowed to sail home and had never repaid. She gave him a bench by the window and a tray of broken escapements. __Each evening she wrote the day's repairs in the ledger, and beside each one she added a small figure, never more than a few céntimos, that she subtracted from his debt without telling him.__ Aroha, for his part, had begun taking orders from a new jeweler across the square, who paid better and asked fewer questions. By autumn he could rebuild a movement faster than she could. When he finally offered to leave for the jeweler's workshop, Consuelo turned the ledger toward him and let him read the last column for himself.

options: It explains why Aroha later chose to accept work from the jeweler across the square.

g.passage: Dried leaves crackled under Nayeli's boots as she climbed the terraces of the plateau's only tea plantation, where she had asked the doctor to meet her. Dvora, the town's sole physician, was already there, holding her notebook flat against the wind. Two people had seen the irrigation flume collapse, and their accounts did not agree. Nayeli, as mayor, wanted one version for the council by Friday. Dvora wanted both written down. She read her notes aloud slowly, pausing at each place where the witnesses diverged, as though the gaps were symptoms worth recording rather than errors to be cleared away. Nayeli listened, tapping her pen, and twice began to summarize before the doctor had finished. Still, when Dvora closed the notebook, Nayeli asked to copy the page, both columns of it. Below them, pickers moved down the rows with baskets on their hips, sorting young buds from older leaves by touch.

g.passage: After every Thursday meeting of our chess club, Bokhee and Pouya descended the same apartment stairwell in Samarkand, four flights, arguing about the endgame they had just played. I lived on the second floor and heard them through my door for years. Their rivalry seemed to me then a kind of performance, loud and slightly ridiculous, two grown men disputing a bishop's move as if a border depended on it. One winter Pouya stopped mentioning a tournament in Tashkent he had told everyone he would win. Bokhee, I learned much later, knew he had withdrawn after the first round and never said a word, not even on the stairs. I used to think their quarrels were the point of the friendship. Now I suspect the quarrels were a cover, a noise loud enough to keep one small silence safe. The bulb on the third landing still flickers, and the building manager still promises to replace it.

g.passage: Who remembers a borrowed tablecloth for nine years? Yaa did, apparently. At my cousin's wedding in a crowded Nairobi hall, she cornered Wanjiru, who had once delivered bread to her flat and now arrived in a pressed suit as the groom's friend. I watched from the cake table, ready to be embarrassed for him. Yaa had been widowed the same winter he borrowed the cloth for his mother's funeral, and I expected her to ask for it back. She did not. She asked only whether it had been enough, whether it had covered the whole table. Wanjiru said it had, with some left over at the edges. For years afterward I told this story as a joke about Yaa's long memory, and people always laughed at the right place. Only lately have I stopped laughing at the part where she asks. Outside, the hired drummers were loading their instruments into a matatu.

g.passage: By the third week of drought, Marta had stopped asking permission to climb to the roof. Her family's rule, older than the building itself, was that the rooftop tank belonged first to the ground-floor garden, and only then to the flats above. Pavel, the surveyor sent from the city ministry in Tbilisi, measured the tank with a folding rule and told her the regulation had changed in 1958: water now went to the residents in equal shares. Marta nodded and kept filling her buckets. Later that afternoon, though, she carried two of them up to the widow on the fourth floor before watering a single tomato. Pavel, writing his report on the steps, crossed out a line and wrote another beneath it. Pigeons gathered along the tank's rim, dipping their beaks where a rivet leaked.

options: It recounts how a surveyor from the city measured a rooftop tank during a drought.

g.passage: Twice a day, at 7:10 and 4:45, the bus to the valley stopped beneath the larches near the house the twins had inherited in the hills above Vienna. Liesel had spent the morning chalking a line down the middle of the hallway, her side, his side, while Anselm carried their mother's books to the kitchen in silence. Twenty years earlier he had promised to come home when their mother fell ill, and he had not. Now, setting the last box down, he said he was sorry. Liesel kept chalking. She did not answer, but when she reached the end of the hall she left a gap in the line, an arm's width, just in front of their mother's door. Outside, the 4:45 groaned up the switchback, its windows yellow, carrying no one who would get off.
g.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A late apology can unsettle a division even when it is not openly accepted.
Two siblings divide the rooms of a house that their mother left to them.

g.passage: Rashid taught oud in the cellar beneath our building in Cairo, and when the pipes burst one February the water rose to his knees in an hour. I helped him carry out the instruments. The finest of them, an old oud from his own teacher, had been left by will not to Rashid but to Tariq, a boy of fifteen who had not spoken in lessons since his father died. Rashid never complained about the will; he simply kept tuning the oud each week and setting it beside Tariq's chair. That morning Tariq waded in before any of us and lifted it above the water first, holding it the way Rashid held it. Neither said anything. Afterward we spread the soaked sheet music across the stairwell railings, where the ink ran in blue threads toward the floor.

options: It recounts how the narrator helped carry instruments out of a flooded cellar.

g.passage: Wet spruce and warm glue: that smell met Anders when he came back to our father's kite yard in Bergen in the spring of 1946. I was eleven then, Marit, his younger sister, and I had kept the yard open with our aunt through the last winter of the war. Father had never written down his recipe for the glue, only shown it, and Anders assumed it had died with him. He watched me stir the pot, add the fish skin, then the vinegar, then a pinch of something I did not name. He asked what it was. I told him I had made that part up when the old supply ran out. He laughed, then asked me to show him again, slowly. Above us the drying kites knocked against the rafters whenever the harbor wind came through the slats.

g.passage: Scotch bonnet and frying plantain filled the boarding-house kitchen in Kingston when Dwayne came in from the ferry, his bag still damp. Bao's mother set out bowls and chopsticks. Wira, from an island far to the south, hesitated, then began eating with his right hand as his family always had. g.passage: Dakar's Corniche was nearly empty at dusk when Yuto and Kwesi locked the shutters of their radio-repair shop for what might be the last time. Their oldest friend lay in the hospital above the promenade, and he believed the shop was thriving; they had told him so at every visit, describing customers who did not exist. Kwesi wanted to keep the story going a little longer. Yuto walked beside him along the sea wall and said nothing for a long while. He had begun to feel that their kindness had become a lantern without oil, something they kept holding up long after it had stopped giving any light. At the hospital stairs he stopped. He would tell their friend the truth, he said, and then they would sit with him for as long as visiting hours allowed. Kwesi looked at the sea before nodding. Fishermen were hauling their painted pirogues up the wet sand.

buttoned to the chin against no weather.
All morning, trucks come through the barrier;
all morning, the scarf stays on,
damp at the collar, itching, kept.
By noon the boy stops checking.
Gulls quarrel over a split crate of apples.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “wears his smile like a borrowed coat” most nearly suggests
options: an expression Jakub adopts for Tane's sake rather than one he feels.
an embarrassment Jakub tries but fails to hide from the other workers.
a plan Jakub has made to return the unwanted scarf to its seller.
a cheerful habit Jakub has shown every morning at the customs gate.
g.explanation: 빌린 외투처럼 미소를 입는다는 표현은 그 미소가 자기 것이 아니라 잠시 걸친 것임을 암시한다. Tane이 Jakub의 얼굴을 살피고, 목도리가 가렵고 젖어도 계속 둘러져 있으며, 정오쯤 소년이 더는 확인하지 않는다는 단서가 이를 뒷받침한다. 따라서 Jakub이 Tane을 위해 꾸민 표정이라는 A가 정답이다. B는 감추기에 실패했다는 점이 지문과 맞지 않고, C의 반품 계획과 D의 평소 습관은 근거가 없다.

seed.conflict: when the plan works and nobody feels better
seed.openingStyle: 대명사 I 또는 We 로 시작
seed.topicSeed: a fishing harbor in Beirut; cousins reunited at a funeral when the plan works and nobody feels better

g.passage: We had planned the scattering for weeks: Salma would bring the boat, Ingeborg would read the letter, and I would keep the younger children away from the edge. Our grandfather had asked that his ashes go into the water off the Beirut harbor where he had fished as a boy, and every detail went exactly as arranged. The wind held. The letter was read without a tremor. Yet when we came back to the dock, Salma tied the rope three times, undoing and redoing the knot, and Ingeborg kept folding the letter into smaller and smaller squares. Our plan had been a bridge built perfectly to the wrong shore. We had prepared for every difficulty except the one of having nothing left to prepare. Along the breakwater, old men cast their lines and waited, rarely speaking.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “a bridge built perfectly to the wrong shore” most nearly suggests
options: a project that failed because the weather on the water changed suddenly.
an arrangement that fully succeeded but did not reach the cousins' grief.
a disagreement among the cousins about where the ashes should be placed.
a journey that carried the family much farther than they had expected.
g.explanation: 지문은 바람도, 편지 낭독도 모든 것이 계획대로 진행되었다고 말한다. 그런데도 Salma는 매듭을 세 번 다시 묶고 Ingeborg는 편지를 계속 접어, 아무도 나아지지 않았음을 보여 준다. 따라서 완벽하게 지었지만 엉뚱한 기슭에 닿은 다리라는 비유는 계획은 성공했으나 슬픔이라는 진짜 문제에는 닿지 못했다는 뜻이므로 정답은 B이다. A는 날씨가 좋았다는 서술과 맞지 않고, C의 갈등과 D의 먼 여정은 지문에 근거가 없다.

seed.conflict: while one of them quietly changes their mind
seed.topicSeed: a rooftop laundry line in Oaxaca; two night-shift coworkers while one of them quietly changes their mind

g.passage: Dario hung his uniforms on the rooftop line every morning at six, after our night shift at the bakery in Oaxaca, and I, Tendai, hung mine beside his. For months he had talked of quitting to drive a taxi with his cousin; he kept the license forms folded in his wallet and showed them to anyone who asked. That spring he spoke of it less. One morning I noticed he had begun pinning a second apron to the line, the white one the head baker gave only to those training for the ovens. He did not mention it, and neither did I. When I finally asked about the taxi, he shrugged and said his plans had gone out with the wash, faded a little each time until he could no longer remember their color. Below us the street vendors were unfolding their umbrellas, one stripe at a time.
g.question: As used in the text, the phrase “his plans had gone out with the wash” most nearly suggests that
options: his plans had been ruined by a sudden accident at the bakery.
he had deliberately thrown away the taxi forms he once carried.
his earlier intention had faded gradually rather than all at once.
he was ashamed that his uniforms had lost their original color.
g.explanation: Dario는 봄이 되며 택시 이야기를 점점 덜 하게 되었고, 어느새 오븐 견습생에게 주는 흰 앞치마를 널기 시작한다. 그가 빨래할 때마다 조금씩 바래 색을 기억할 수 없게 되었다고 덧붙이는 것도 점진적인 변화를 가리킨다. 따라서 이 비유는 이전의 계획이 한순간이 아니라 서서히 사라졌다는 뜻이므로 정답은 C이다. A의 갑작스러운 사고와 B의 의도적인 폐기는 점진성과 맞지 않고, D는 빨래라는 소재를 문자 그대로 읽었다.
